stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department experiencing progressive fatigue and lightheadedness. A week prior, he suffered an acute upper respiratory infection, and has since noted worsening dyspnea with mild physical exertion. He has no significant chronic medical illnesses and is a lifelong nonsmoker. Clinical examination shows body temperature of 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure of 80/60 mm Hg, and regular pulse at 120/min. His peripheral radial pulse weakens significantly and becomes impalpable during deep inspiration. Physical examination reveals distended neck veins with clear lung fields bilaterally. Which condition is the most probable cause of this clinical presentation?

explanations.A: Acute coronary syndrome typically presents with substernal chest pressure, autonomic symptoms, and crackles if complicated by cardiogenic shock, without marked pulsus paradoxus.
explanations.B: Myocarditis commonly induces diffuse left ventricular contractility impairment and heart failure, sometimes featuring pulsus alternans rather than classic pulsus paradoxus.
explanations.C: Viral pericarditis complicated by pericardial effusion can cause tamponade, marked by Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, distant sounds) and pulsus paradoxus from ventricular interdependence.
explanations.D: Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic process causing pericardial fibrosis over months, rather than an acute post-viral hemodynamic collapse.
explanations.E: Early septic shock represents a distributive state with warm extremities, widened pulse pressure, and bounding pulses.
explanations.F: Tension pneumothorax manifests with absent ipsilateral breath sounds, tympanitic percussion note, and contralateral tracheal shift.

generalExplanation: This patient displays classic signs of cardiac tamponade: hypotension, tachycardia, jugular venous distension with clear lung sounds, and pulsus paradoxus (loss of palpable arterial pulse upon inspiration). This acute tamponade likely arose secondary to viral pericarditis with rapid pericardial fluid collection. In tamponade, limited pericardial compliance enforces rigid intracardiac volume boundaries; inspiratory augmentation of right heart venous filling shifts the interventricular septum leftward, encroaching on the left ventricular chamber, sharply reducing stroke volume and lowering systemic systolic pressure by >10 mm Hg.
educationalObjective: Cardiac tamponade produces Beck's triad (systemic hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds) alongside pulsus paradoxus (an exaggerated decrease in systolic blood pressure greater than 10 mm Hg during normal inspiration), resulting from exaggerated ventricular interdependence inside a noncompliant pericardial sac.

stem: A 33-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and worsening exertional dyspnea over the preceding 6 months. One year ago, he was treated with parenteral antibiotics for infective endocarditis associated with intravenous drug abuse, and has remained abstinent since. He takes no medications. Auscultation demonstrates an early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Bilateral carotid artery examinations reveal abrupt upstrokes followed by sudden collapse. Firm auscultation over the femoral artery with stethoscope compression reveals a characteristic systolic and diastolic murmur (to-and-fro bruit). Cardiac catheterization is most likely to record which set of intracardiac and vascular pressures (mm Hg)?

explanations.A: A left ventricular systolic pressure significantly exceeding aortic systolic pressure indicates left ventricular outflow tract obstruction or aortic stenosis, which produces pulsus parvus et tardus.
explanations.B: These parameters correspond to standard, physiological resting intracardiac and aortic pressures.
explanations.C: Isolated elevation of LV end-diastolic pressure with preserved systolic levels characterizes chronic compensated left ventricular systolic or diastolic failure.
explanations.D: Chronic aortic regurgitation features widened pulse pressure, high peak systolic aortic and LV pressures from compensatory stroke volume, and decreased aortic diastolic pressure alongside elevated LV diastolic pressure from diastolic backflow.
explanations.E: Concomitant elevation of aortic systolic and diastolic pressures without an transvalvular systolic gradient represents systemic hypertension.

generalExplanation: The patient exhibits pathognomonic physical examination signs of chronic severe aortic regurgitation (AR) following endocarditis-mediated valvular damage. Manifestations include bounding 'water-hammer' pulses (Corrigan sign), Duroziez sign (systolic and diastolic murmurs over compressed femoral vessels), and a prominent pulse pressure. Diastolic regurgitant flow through the incompetent aortic valve into the left ventricle decreases aortic diastolic pressure while raising LV end-diastolic volume and filling pressure. The resulting eccentric ventricular hypertrophy accommodates an increased total stroke volume, driving marked aortic systolic hypertension.
educationalObjective: Aortic regurgitation triggers diastolic regurgitation into the left ventricle, causing eccentric hypertrophy and elevated stroke volume. Typical hemodynamic tracings demonstrate increased systolic aortic and left ventricular pressures, significantly depressed aortic diastolic pressure, and elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, creating marked pulse pressure widening.

stem: A 38-year-old woman collapses unexpectedly at home and is pronounced dead upon arrival at the hospital. Postmortem macroscopic inspection demonstrates an acute occlusive thrombus overlying an ulcerated atheroma in the left anterior descending coronary artery. Examination of the heart also reveals thickened mitral valve leaflets studded with multiple sterile, verrucous vegetations distributed on both the atrial and ventricular surfaces, accompanied by arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis. Renal histological evaluation identifies diffuse subendothelial immune complex deposits producing 'wire-loop' lesions along glomerular capillary basement membranes. Which underlying medical disorder was this patient afflicted with?

explanations.A: Infective endocarditis generates large, destructive, friable vegetations with active bacterial colonization, preferentially confined to the upstream flow surface of valvular cusps.
explanations.B: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels associated with asthma, allergic rhinitis, and prominent peripheral eosinophilia.
explanations.C: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis features necrotizing granulomas of the upper/lower respiratory tracts and pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis without Libman-Sacks vegetations.
explanations.D: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) produces accelerated atherogenesis, arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (wire-loop capillary thickening), and verrucous Libman-Sacks endocarditis on both leaflet sides.
explanations.E: Buerger disease is a segmental inflammatory vasculitis of medium and small peripheral extremities strongly linked to cigarette smoking.

generalExplanation: The constellation of accelerated premature coronary artery atherosclerosis, verrucous Libman-Sacks endocarditis (sterile, small vegetations on both leaflet faces), and capillary basement membrane 'wire-loop' thickening on renal biopsy strongly characterizes systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Libman-Sacks vegetations consist of immune complexes, fibrin, mononuclear cells, and platelet aggregates that adhere to both the inflow and outflow aspects of valve cusps. Accelerated atherosclerosis secondary to chronic autoimmune vascular inflammation is a premier cause of premature coronary thrombosis in SLE.
educationalObjective: Cardiovascular features of systemic lupus erythematosus encompass accelerated atherosclerosis, acute pericarditis, and verrucous Libman-Sacks endocarditis characterized by small, sterile vegetations on both sides of valve leaflets. Renal involvement typically features diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with subendothelial wire-loop deposits.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a long-standing history of exertional breathlessness presents following a syncopal episode. Examination reveals a slow-rising carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a harsh crescendo-decrescendo midsystolic murmur maximal at the right second intercostal space with a soft S2. Echocardiography establishes critical calcific aortic stenosis. Two months later, he is brought urgently to the emergency ward with acute severe dyspnea and palpitations. His blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg and heart rate is 130/min with an irregularly irregular pulse. ECG confirms new-onset atrial fibrillation. Pulmonary examination and chest radiography reveal acute pulmonary edema. Which hemodynamic change directly triggered this sudden deterioration?

options.B: Sudden decrease in left ventricular preload
options.C: Sudden decrease in left ventricular systolic function
options.D: Sudden increase in left ventricular afterload
options.E: Sudden increase in left ventricular filling

explanations.A: Right ventricular dysfunction leads to systemic venous congestion (jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema) rather than sudden acute pulmonary edema.
explanations.B: In concentric LV hypertrophy due to chronic severe aortic stenosis, ventricular compliance is low, rendering LV filling highly dependent on atrial contraction ('atrial kick'). Loss of coordinated atrial systole in acute AF abruptly slashes LV preload, precipitating hypotension and upstream pulmonary congestion.
explanations.C: In the absence of acute myocardial ischemia, intrinsic cardiomyocyte contractility remains unchanged; the reduction in cardiac output is driven by reduced preload.
explanations.D: Valvular afterload in chronic degenerative aortic stenosis is determined by anatomical orifice narrowing that progresses over years rather than acutely changing.
explanations.E: Left ventricular filling is critically compromised, not enhanced, due to both loss of the atrial contraction boost and shortened diastolic filling periods at tachycardia.

generalExplanation: Patients with severe chronic aortic stenosis develop significant concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, creating a stiff, noncompliant left ventricular chamber with impaired passive diastolic filling. Consequently, effective late-diastolic active atrial contraction (the atrial kick) supplies up to 30-40% of ventricular filling volume. The sudden onset of atrial fibrillation eliminates coordinated atrial systole while rapid ventricular response curtails diastolic filling time. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume and stroke volume abruptly collapse, leading to profound systemic hypotension and severe retrograde hydrostatic pressure transmission into pulmonary capillaries, causing acute pulmonary edema.
educationalObjective: In patients with severe aortic valve stenosis and noncompliant concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, active atrial systole is vital for adequate ventricular preload. Acute onset of atrial fibrillation ablates the atrial kick, sharply reducing left ventricular filling and forward stroke volume, leading to systemic hypotension and pulmonary edema.

stem: A 42-year-old male programmer presents to the emergency room following a syncopal event preceded by palpitations. He takes no prescription medications and denies history of ethanol, tobacco, or illicit substance use. He spends the vast majority of his time indoors. Vital signs are normal with no orthostatic blood pressure changes. Physical examination shows an enlarged, nontender liver margin and generalized dark slate-bronze cutaneous hyperpigmentation. Cardiac rhythm monitoring discloses sinus node arrest with junctional escape beats, and echocardiogram indicates impaired left ventricular diastolic relaxation. Which process is the underlying cause of this patient's clinical state?

explanations.A: Cardiac amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, but characteristic non-cardiac features include macroglossia, periorbital ecchymoses, nephrotic syndrome, and peripheral neuropathy.
explanations.B: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) features hyperpigmentation from ACTH/MSH co-secretion, but causes hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia without hepatomegaly.
explanations.C: Sarcoidosis produces noncaseating granulomas that can infiltrate the myocardium, but pulmonary infiltrates, hilar adenopathy, and cutaneous nodules are standard.
explanations.D: Hereditary hemochromatosis involves HFE gene mutations; HLA gene mutations are not the molecular cause of pathological cellular injury.
explanations.E: Excessive intestinal iron absorption in hereditary hemochromatosis leads to hemosiderin and ferritin deposition in hepatocytes, skin melanocytes, and cardiomyocytes, driving restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy and sick sinus syndrome.
explanations.F: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe disease) is an infantile or juvenile glycogen storage disease presenting with massive cardiomegaly and hypotonia.

generalExplanation: This patient's constellation of syncope, sinus node dysfunction, left ventricular diastolic dysfunction, hepatomegaly, and bronze skin pigmentation in a middle-aged male points directly to hereditary hemochromatosis. Uncontrolled intestinal iron absorption due to mutations in the HFE gene leads to systemic iron overload, with excessive iron depositing into cardiomyocytes, hepatocytes, endocrine organs, and skin. Cardiac hemochromatosis initially produces restrictive diastolic dysfunction that progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy and cardiac conduction system disruptions (such as sick sinus syndrome and atrioventricular block). Prussian blue staining demonstrates coarse golden-brown hemosiderin granules within cardiomyocytes.
educationalObjective: Hereditary hemochromatosis is characterized by excessive intestinal iron absorption leading to parenchymal iron accumulation. Cardiac involvement is mediated by direct myocyte iron toxicity and deposition, presenting early as restrictive diastolic dysfunction and conduction disturbances (eg, sinus node dysfunction), and later as dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the clinic after missing a routine cardiology review for congestive heart failure. He explains that persistent gastrointestinal upset kept him homebound. Review of symptoms reveals altered color vision (yellow-green halos), loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and loose stools over the past 2 weeks. His chronic systolic heart failure has historically been maintained on a multidrug regimen. If the underlying etiology of this patient's acute symptoms is not corrected, which complication is most imminent and lethal?

explanations.A: Angioedema is a dangerous adverse reaction linked to ACE inhibitors due to bradykinin accumulation, but does not present with xanthopsia or gastrointestinal toxicity.
explanations.B: Digoxin toxicity generates increased automaticity and delayed afterdepolarizations along with slowed AV conduction, posing high risks of fatal cardiac arrhythmias (eg, bidirectional VT, ventricular fibrillation, severe bradycardia).
explanations.C: Bronchoconstriction is associated with nonselective beta-blockers in patients with reactive airway disease.
explanations.D: Hypotension can accompany severe volume depletion, but life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias represent the most critical lethal outcome of digoxin poisoning.
explanations.E: Pulmonary edema indicates decompensated congestive heart failure; the patient's current presentation reflects systemic drug toxicity.

generalExplanation: The combination of constitutional symptoms, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and classic xanthopsia (disturbed yellow-green tint and halo vision) in a patient treated for heart failure indicates chronic digoxin toxicity. Digoxin has a notoriously narrow therapeutic window. Renal impairment, hypokalemia (which increases myocardial digoxin binding), and hypomagnesemia commonly precipitate toxicity. While gastrointestinal and visual disturbances serve as warning signals, the most dangerous and lethal sequela of digoxin toxicity is cardiac arrhythmia, which can range from junctional escape rhythms and paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with AV block to bidirectional ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation.
educationalObjective: Digoxin toxicity manifests with nonspecific gastrointestinal complaints (anorexia, nausea, vomiting), neurological signs (fatigue, confusion), and specific color vision changes (yellow-green halos, xanthopsia). The most dangerous and life-threatening complication is the induction of fatal cardiac arrhythmias.

stem: A 23-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of recurrent substernal chest tightness triggered by exertion, such as jogging or stair climbing, which remits within 10 minutes of rest. He notes mild accompanying exertional shortness of breath but denies loss of consciousness. Family history is remarkable for a paternal uncle who died suddenly of an unexpected cardiac event at age 35. Blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg and regular pulse is 70/min. Physical examination shows a sustained apical impulse and a dynamic crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left sternal border; the murmur is faint while supine but accentuates substantially upon abrupt standing. Which pharmacologic agent must be avoided in managing this patient?

explanations.A: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent utilized when needed to suppress symptomatic atrial or ventricular arrhythmias in HCM.
explanations.B: Disopyramide is a class IA antiarrhythmic with negative inotropic actions that decreases left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) dynamic gradients.
explanations.C: Nitrates (such as isosorbide dinitrate) cause profound venodilation and arteriolar relaxation, decreasing LV preload and afterload; this diminishes LV end-diastolic chamber volume and drastically exacerbates dynamic LVOT obstruction.
explanations.D: Beta-blockers (metoprolol) are first-line therapy; they prolong diastole to boost LV filling and decrease myocardial contractility, reducing outflow obstruction.
explanations.E: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil) act as negative inotropes and chronotropes, helping to relieve dynamic LVOT gradients.

generalExplanation: This patient's young age, family history of premature sudden cardiac death, exertional angina, and systolic murmur that intensifies upon standing (due to reduced venous return/preload) are classic for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). In HCM, asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve leaflet create dynamic subaortic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO). Medications that decrease ventricular blood volume—including venodilators/nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate, nitroglycerin), dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and diuretics—worsen LVOTO by allowing the hypertrophied septum and anterior mitral leaflet to coapt more tightly during systole.
educationalObjective: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy worsens with reductions in left ventricular blood volume. Vasodilators (such as isosorbide dinitrate, nitroglycerin, and dihydropyridines) and diuretics decrease preload and afterload, exacerbating the obstruction, and are generally contraindicated.

stem: A 6-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department for severe lethargy of several hours' duration. His mother reports that he is usually vigorous and active. Full-term birth history was unremarkable. Body temperature is normal, blood pressure is 70/44 mm Hg, pulse is 240/min, and respirations are 52/min. The infant appears pale and diaphoretic with capillary refill time under 2 seconds. Auscultation reveals clear breath sounds bilaterally and no murmurs. ECG shows a regular rhythm at 240 beats/min with narrow QRS complexes and non-identifiable P waves. Which hemodynamic mechanism is primarily responsible for this infant's hypotension?

explanations.A: Hypovolemic shock results from extracellular fluid loss (diarrhea, hemorrhage, dehydration) and features delayed capillary refill, sunken fontanelles, and poor skin turgor.
explanations.B: Primary contractile failure occurs in viral myocarditis or congenital metabolic heart defects, which typically manifest with heart murmurs, hepatomegaly, and pulmonary crackles.
explanations.C: Distributive shock (septic or anaphylactic) features peripheral vasodilation, warm flushed skin early on, and fever or allergic triggers.
explanations.D: Left-to-right shunts (large VSD, PDA) produce significant biventricular volume overload, crackles, and distinctive murmurs rather than paroxysmal narrow-complex SVT.
explanations.E: In extreme sustained tachycardias (infantile SVT >220/min), the ventricular diastolic filling interval is drastically truncated, impairing stroke volume and forward cardiac output, resulting in systemic hypotension.

generalExplanation: The infant's presentation of marked tachycardia (240/min), regular narrow QRS complexes, and hidden P waves is diagnostic of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), most commonly caused by an AV nodal reentrant circuit or accessory pathway. While infants can tolerate brief periods of tachycardia, sustained extreme rates severely shorten the cardiac cycle—predominantly at the expense of diastole. Because coronary perfusion and ventricular relaxation and filling take place during diastole, ventricular end-diastolic volume drops precipitously. Stroke volume collapses, leading to secondary hypotension, tissue hypoperfusion, and clinical lethargy.
educationalObjective: Supraventricular tachycardia presents with high, regular heart rates with narrow QRS complexes. Sustained extreme heart rates critically shorten ventricular diastole, drastically compromising ventricular end-diastolic filling, stroke volume, and cardiac output, resulting in systemic hypotension.

stem: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled chronic hypertension is brought to the emergency department suffering from sudden-onset breathlessness and dry cough that prevents him from sleeping recumbent. Blood pressure is 192/102 mm Hg and regular heart rate is 92/min. Cardiac auscultation reveals an S4 gallop, and pulmonary examination shows bilateral basal crackles. An intravenous infusion of nitroglycerin is initiated, leading to rapid and marked clinical improvement. Which combination of vascular and intracardiac hemodynamic changes is most likely induced by this medication?

options.A: LVEDP: No effect | Peripheral venous capacitance: ↑ | SVR: ↓
options.B: LVEDP: ↓ | Peripheral venous capacitance: ↑ | SVR: No effect
options.F: LVEDP: ↑ | Peripheral venous capacitance: No effect | SVR: ↓

explanations.A: Nitroglycerin directly relieves pulmonary venous congestion by shifting blood volume into capacitive veins, markedly lowering LVEDP.
explanations.B: At therapeutic doses, particularly parenteral infusions used in hypertensive emergencies, nitroglycerin acts on arterial smooth muscle as well, causing modest reductions in systemic vascular resistance.
explanations.C: Constriction of capacitance veins and arterial beds reflects alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation, the opposite of nitrate pharmacodynamics.
explanations.D: Nitrates act predominantly as venodilators, expanding systemic venous capacitance, which decreases central venous return (preload) and lowers left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP). At higher intravenous doses, they also promote arteriolar vasodilation, decreasing systemic vascular resistance (afterload).
explanations.E: Nitrates increase, rather than decrease, venous capacitance via cGMP-mediated venous smooth muscle relaxation.
explanations.F: LVEDP is consistently reduced by venodilation.
explanations.G: Vasoconstrictive physiology increases afterload and filling pressures, aggravating acute heart failure.

generalExplanation: This patient has acute hypertensive cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Intravenous nitroglycerin provides rapid symptom relief primarily through venodilation, which increases peripheral venous capacitance and pools blood in large capacitance veins. This substantially decreases right and left ventricular venous return (preload), reducing left ventricular end-diastolic volume and pressure (LVEDP) and alleviating pulmonary capillary hydrostatic transudation. Concurrently, particularly at intravenous infusion rates, nitroglycerin promotes moderate arteriolar relaxation, lowering systemic vascular resistance (SVR/afterload) and decreasing myocardial wall tension.
educationalObjective: Organic nitrates are potent venodilators that increase peripheral venous capacitance, thereby decreasing ventricular preload and lowering left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and volume. At therapeutic parenteral doses, they also modestly dilate systemic arterioles, reducing systemic vascular resistance and cardiac afterload.

stem: A 48-year-old man visits the outpatient clinic for a six-month follow-up of hypercholesterolemia. Despite rigorous adherence to an approved diet and aerobic exercise regimen, his serum lipid panel shows a persistent LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL. His father developed coronary artery disease in his 50s and has diabetes mellitus. The patient's blood pressure is 126/70 mm Hg and BMI is 33.1 kg/m². Physical examination is unremarkable. HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) therapy is planned. Which baseline laboratory study should be performed before initiating this medication?

explanations.A: Apo-B quantification measures circulating atherogenic lipoprotein particles, but does not identify drug contraindications or baseline organ toxicity risks.
explanations.B: Statins do not exert myelosuppressive or hematologic adverse effects.
explanations.C: Lipoprotein lipase activity assessment is diagnostic for familial chylomicronemia syndrome, which presents with severe hypertriglyceridemia, not isolated elevated LDL.
explanations.D: Statins can induce drug-induced hepatotoxicity with elevated serum aminotransferases (AST/ALT); obtaining baseline liver transaminase levels prior to treatment initiation is standard clinical practice.
explanations.E: Although cholesterol serves as the molecular precursor for adrenocortical steroidogenesis, statins do not impair adrenal hormone synthesis in clinical practice.
explanations.F: Routine monitoring of renal function or baseline creatine kinase in asymptomatic individuals is not recommended prior to initiating statins unless significant muscle disorders exist.

generalExplanation: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) are competitive inhibitors of the rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis and represent the first-line lipid-lowering pharmacological therapy for cardiovascular prevention. Primary adverse drug reactions include myopathy (myalgias, myositis, and rarely rhabdomyolysis) and chemical hepatitis. Clinically significant elevations in hepatic transaminases (AST and ALT greater than three times the upper limit of normal) occur in under 1% of patients and are generally reversible. Baseline evaluation of serum liver transaminases is universally recommended before beginning statin therapy.
educationalObjective: Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) frequently cause mild transaminase elevation and can precipitate drug-induced hepatitis or myopathy. Baseline hepatic transaminases (AST/ALT) should always be measured prior to beginning statin therapy.

stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought by her parents for a routine adolescent health evaluation. Physical growth parameters demonstrate height at the 5th percentile and weight at the 25th percentile. Blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. Physical examination shows a short webbed neck, widely spaced nipples across a broad shield chest, and bilateral shortening of the fourth metacarpal bones. Cardiac auscultation reveals an early systolic ejection click followed by a soft systolic murmur. Which congenital lesion is most likely present on her echocardiogram?

explanations.A: Atrial septal defects (ostium secundum) and atrioventricular canal defects (endocardial cushion defects) are the classic cardiac abnormalities associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
explanations.B: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is most frequently associated with a bicuspid aortic valve (present in up to 30% of patients) and coarctation of the aorta.
explanations.C: Mitral stenosis is typically acquired via post-streptococcal rheumatic carditis and produces an opening snap with a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur.
explanations.D: Mitral valve prolapse occurs with connective tissue matrix diseases such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
explanations.E: Patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur, predominantly observed in premature neonates or congenital rubella infection.
explanations.F: Ventricular septal defects are common in trisomies 13, 18, and 21, manifesting as harsh holosystolic murmurs at the left lower sternal border.

generalExplanation: The patient's somatic features—short stature, webbed neck, broad shield chest, and shortened fourth metacarpal bones—are classic manifestations of Turner syndrome (45,XO). Congenital cardiovascular anomalies are present in over 50% of females with Turner syndrome. Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is by far the most common congenital defect (found in ~30% of patients), followed closely by aortic coarctation. A nonstenotic bicuspid aortic valve typically generates an early systolic ejection click heard over the right second intercostal space; over decades, the anatomically abnormal valve is prone to progressive calcification, premature stenosis, and infective endocarditis.
educationalObjective: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is strongly associated with congenital aortic and left-sided cardiac anomalies, the most common of which is a bicuspid aortic valve (seen in up to 30% of cases), followed by coarctation of the aorta.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a four-day history of high spiking fever, dyspnea, and profound malaise. Temperature is 39.4 C (102.9 F), blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg, and regular pulse is 102/min. Precordial auscultation detects a newly audible, high-pitched blowing holosystolic murmur maximal at the cardiac apex radiating to the left axilla. Dermatologic inspection reveals multiple flat, nontender, erythematous macular lesions distributed across the plantar aspect of both feet as shown in the exhibit. Which pathological mechanism accounts for these cutaneous lesions?

explanations.A: Benign vascular proliferations like bacillary angiomatosis or Kaposi sarcoma appear as raised violaceous nodules or papules rather than acute planar septic macules.
explanations.B: Granulomatous skin lesions are characteristic of leprosy, miliary tuberculosis, or cutaneous sarcoidosis.
explanations.C: Osler nodes are painful, violaceous nodules located on the pads of the digits caused by immune complex deposition with dermal vasculitis.
explanations.D: Janeway lesions are painless, erythematous macules on the palms and soles caused by septic embolization of valvular vegetations that form microabscesses in cutaneous microvessels.
explanations.E: Primary fungal (sporotrichosis) or cutaneous bacterial inoculation causes localized papules, pustules, or ulcerations with sporotrichoid lymphangitic spread.

generalExplanation: The patient's acute bacteremic illness, high fever, and newly appeared apical holosystolic murmur (indicative of acute mitral regurgitation) are typical of infective endocarditis (IE). The painless, flat, erythematous macules on his soles are Janeway lesions. Janeway lesions represent true vascular phenomena caused by septic microembolization originating from valvular vegetations; histologically, they consist of microabscesses with neutrophilic infiltration, bacteria, and microvascular necrosis. In contrast, Osler nodes are painful, raised nodules on the pulp of the fingers and toes caused by immunologic immune-complex vasculitis.
educationalObjective: Janeway lesions are nontender, erythematous macules located on the palms and soles in infective endocarditis. They are caused by septic embolization from infected cardiac vegetations leading to cutaneous microabscess formation.
